newsitem.title: UK: UK pension funds thrived in '96 - WM Company survey.
newsitem.headline: UK pension funds thrived in '96 - WM Company survey.

text.p: UK pension funds thrived in 1996, fuelled by strong equity market returns from the home market, North America and Continental Europe, a survey of 1,400 pension funds by actuaries and consultants WM Company shows.
Pension funds shrugged off uncertainties towards the end of the year and showed an average overall return of over 11 percent, well ahead of retail price inflation of two percent.

That did not match the "spectacular" performance of 1995 which brought returns of 19 percent, but WM, which monitors the investment performance of over 75 percent of the UK pension fund market, said the UK offered "anything but doom and gloom" ahead.

"UK equities continue to stride forward," said Peter Warrington, analyst at WM. "Our survey shows that UK equities provided a return of 17 percent, with the very active managers outperforming the FTSE-All Share Index." Historically active managers have underperformed the index.
Amongst foreign markets, the top equity performer was North America, with a 13 percent return. Japan trailed badly with a negative 22 percent return.
But sterling, up eight percent on the dollar and around 16 percent in Europe and Japan, depressed returns for UK local investors to 13 percent in the US and 12 percent in Europe.
UK pension funds ran down their investment in the US to around 3.8 percent even as the market climbed, but recouped potential losses through a high exposure to Europe and a low exposure to Japan.
WM noted that smaller UK pension funds did almost 0.5 percent better than the very large funds because of limited commitment to property and better results in UK equities.
The funds currently have a high cash weighting, having taken profits in the UK and North America, and there is a steady flow of investment into index-linked securities and "more surprisingly", Japan.

"The high cash holdings support the widespread belief that the major equity markets, particularly the UK and US, are over valued," noted Warrington. "Funds may be waiting for a downturn before returning to buy at lower levels."
UK pension funds still have over 75 percent of their assets in equities, with the UK over 50 percent of average fund value.
While total exposure to world equity markets has fallen back to the level of 1991 it remains well ahead of anything experienced in the 1980s, WM said.
